newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Merrill plans investment trusts in Japan.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Merrill plans investment trusts in Japan.

text.p: Competition is set to heat up as Japan's "Big Bang" reforms open the way for its investment trust market to expand, but Merrill Lynch is betting brand recognition and experience back home will ensure success.

"Nobody knows exactly what will happen in this market but until you know what the reality is, you have to go there," Hidemi Fukuhara, president of Tokyo's Merrill Lynch International Capital Management Co Ltd, told Reuters in an interview on Friday.

Merrill Lynch International Capital Management, a unit of Merrill Lynch Asset Management LP, plans to apply in two or three weeks for a licence to launch investment trusts, similar to U.S. mutual funds, in Japan and intends to start business in the sector within this year, Fukuhara said.

Like other foreign and domestic financial firms, Merrill -- now the number four player in America's vast U.S. mutual fund arena -- is betting that Japan's investment trust business will expand sharply as Tokyo implements "Big Bang" reforms aimed at boosting competition in its long-protected financial sector.
But just how big will Japan's investment trust market, currently worth about 45 trillion yen ($394 billion) against about 200 trillion yen ($1.75 trillion) in the United States, be in five years?

"It's a very difficult question. All I can say is that it should expand dramatically," Fukuhara said. "The key initiative in the 'Big Bang' is how to diversify individual financial assets. One key area in which not only the government but also a lot of players in the industry and hopefully individuals themselves are expecting more convenience and product variety is in the investment trust area," Fukuhara said.

Fukuhara dismissed concerns that conservative Japanese investors might shun investment trusts in favour of safer bank deposits. "Every investor in the world...wants to make money with minimal risk. So in that sense there is no difference between Japanese investors and U.S. investors," he said.

But changes to Japanese tax law to allow U.S.-style "defined contribution" pension plans as an alternative to defined benefit plans which provide a guaranteed return are needed if Japan's investment trust market is to see the explosive growth seen in the United States, Fukuhara said.
Meanwhile, expectations of sharp growth in the investment trust market are prompting several foreign firms such as U.S. top mutual fund player Fidelity Investments to eye the sector.

Domestic players are also gearing up for the overall asset management market to take-off. Two Nomura group asset management firms are set to merge in October 1997 to form one of the world's biggest asset management companies.
Merrill Lynch, however, is betting that its well-known name in Japan combined with its success in the U.S. mutual fund market will give it an edge as competition here intensifies.
"Everyone, even players who don't have an actual presence in the asset management business in the States, are seeking a chance to build and expand their business here," Fukuhara said.
"But the reality is that Merrill Lynch is the only securities firm with a certain presence in Japan that has also had a successful experience in the business in the States."

Merrill Lynch International Capital Management has added about eight new staff to the 10 on board when Fukuhara assumed his new post in April and plans to raise the total to at least 25, Fukuhara said. Merrill intends to launch one fund worth $200 million to $300 million this year and a total of about six funds in its first year in the business.

The U.S. firm will not, however, market the investment trusts directly but will do so through one or more Japanese brokers and perhaps domestic banks, once they are allowed to distribute such products after next April, Fukuda said.
A spokesman for Merrill Lynch Japan, meanwhile, denied rumours that the U.S. brokerage might acquire a Japanese brokerage to get into the retail securities sector here.
"There are some rumours but there is no plan at this point to buy or merge with any Japanese firm," said Toru Ichikawa, vice president of marketing and communications at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.
Fukuhara said that in his personal opinion U.S. brokerages were unlikely to acquire a Japanese securities house given the domestic firms' low profitability compared to American rivals.
"As long as U.S. corporations care about the reaction from shareholders, they won't take that action until Japanese brokerages' profitability increases," he said. ($1=114 yen)
